newsitem.title: FRANCE: French lender defies "wind-down" plans with profit.
newsitem.headline: French lender defies "wind-down" plans with profit.

text.p: French property lender Credit Foncier de France said on Wednesday it could post a hefty full-year profit, fuelling controversy about government plans to wind it down on grounds it faces collapse.
The bank, once France's second-biggest bond issuer after the state, said second-half earnings could match its surprise 402 million franc ($76.3 million) first-half profit, barring fresh provisions.

"The expected result for the second half of 1996 could be in line with that of the first half," the group said. Net banking income would be better than forecast due to a drop in interest rates and operating costs should fall by eight percent, it said. The overall risk charge should also be lower than expected.

The lender's bullish profit forecast came after several hundred union members invaded a board meeting late on Tuesday and refused to allow directors to leave for several hours to press home their demands to keep the lender alive.
Union officials seized on the profit forecast as proof that the 144-year-old lender was viable and stuck by their predictions it would report a one billion franc profit this year.

The government's plan "is dead", said a spokesman for unions at the group. "Instead of announcing provisions, we're making money. What we need is time to find a buyer." The unions have demanded a year's grace to seek a purchaser.

Such a climbdown would be another embarrassing policy U-turn for Prime Minister Alain Juppe's centre-right government after it pulled the privatisation of electronics group Thomson on Wednesday and French banking network CIC last month.

The government announced in July a "managed wind-down" of Credit Foncier saying there was no way to save the lender after it reported a 1995 loss of 10.8 billion francs due to 14 billion francs of provisions for risky property loans and investments.
The plan outraged unions and shareholders which accused Credit Foncier of loading the books with losses, making its failure inevitable.
Under the government's plan, state bank CDC has launched a 70 franc per share offer for Credit Foncier, once a "widows and orphans" stock which traded at 450 francs a share.

The plan calls for its commercial activities and low-cost housing loan portfolio to be spun off. The lender would be reduced to a shell company and placed in a state holding firm that would ensure that bonds in its name were honoured.

The unions' anger on Tuesday had been stoked by Finance Minister Jean Arthuis's remarks to parliament expressing amazement that the banking commission was still allowing Credit Foncier to lend money and pledging to "sort out the situation".
On Wednesday however, unions and a source close to Credit Foncier said Arthuis's office told them he would not seek to stop it lending money which would spell its death.

The group ran into trouble with the collapse in property prices and loss of a state monopoly to sell low-cost mortgages. It is private but top management is appointed by the government due to its status as a specialised financial institution. ($ = 5.270 French Francs)
